fig1_condenser_duty.svg: A condenser takes the two-phase turbine exhaust and returns saturated liquid for the pump. The heat it must reject per kilogram is $h_2-h_3$ (condenser_heat_per_mass), linear in the incoming quality through the lever rule (enthalpy_two_phase). The magnitude is the striking part: at the typical exhaust quality $x=0.88$ it is 2115 kJ/kg — comparable to everything the boiler added — because almost all of it is latent heat that never became work. quality_from_h recovers $x$ from a measured enthalpy.
fig2_cooling_water.svg: The consequence of that duty. Rejecting 300 MW into cooling water (heat_transfer_rate / heat_rejected supply the signed and unsigned forms) needs a flow of $\dot Q/(c_p\Delta T)$, so the permitted temperature rise sets the size of the circuit: 9.0 tonnes per second for an 8 K rise, falling to 4.8 t/s if 15 K is allowed. Thermal-discharge limits on rivers therefore translate directly into pump and intake sizing, and are a large part of why power stations are built beside big water.
